big: Some funds hire analysts to pick winning shares. Others simply copy a list. The copying kind charges far less, and over twenty years that gap can matter more than any one pick.

lines: If index funds are so cheap, why do you sell active funds?
Fair challenge. First see what an index fund really holds and what cost does over twenty years, then I will answer.

rows.name: Index fund: same shares, same weights

alt: Three bars: an index, an index fund holding the same shares in the same shares, and an active fund holding different weights
caps: An index is a list of shares with set weights. Here is a made-up index of four shares.
An index fund holds the same shares in the same weights. No analyst, no guessing.
An active fund's manager picks and weights shares differently, hoping to beat the list.
The index fund aims to match the index, not beat it. That is passive investing.

alt: Bars comparing yearly cost and final value of ₹10 lakh in an index fund at 0.2 percent and an active fund at 1.5 percent
caps: Assume both funds earn 12% a year before costs. This is an assumption to isolate the effect of cost.
Index fund: 0.2% a year, or ₹2,000 on ₹10 lakh. Active fund: 1.5%, or ₹15,000.
After 20 years ₹10 lakh grows to about ₹93.1 lakh in the index fund and ₹73.7 lakh in the active fund.
Same pre-cost return. The ₹19 lakh gap comes only from cost compounding.

h: What passive does and does not mean
title: Fair claims, and unfair ones
stops: Copies an index, with no stock picking
Return is about the index minus costs
Cannot fall when the market falls
alt: A shield with true and false claims about passive funds
caps: A passive fund copies an index and costs less, with no research team to pay.
But it falls when its index falls. Passive means low cost, not low risk.
And it is not guaranteed to beat active funds. In some areas a good manager has more room to add value.

q: Two funds each earn 12% a year before costs. One charges 0.2% and the other 1.5%. Rohan invests ₹10 lakh in each for 20 years. About how much more does the cheaper fund leave?
opts: About ₹2.6 lakh, which is 1.3% of ₹10 lakh for 20 years
About ₹19 lakh, since the drag compounds each year
About ₹13,000, which is one year of the cost gap
Almost nothing, as both funds earned 12% before costs
why: That adds up simple costs and misses compounding. A lower yearly return also shrinks every later year's base.
At 11.8% the index fund grows to about ₹93 lakh, and at 10.5% the active fund reaches about ₹74 lakh. Gap about ₹19 lakh.
The yearly gap is 1.3% of ₹10 lakh, which is ₹13,000 in year one. It keeps growing as the pile grows.
Costs come out of the return. Equal returns before costs do not mean equal returns after them.

q: An index returned 14.0% in a year. Meena's index fund on that index returned 13.8%. Where did the 0.2% go?
opts: The manager's poor stock picks, which pulled the fund down
The fund holds different shares from the index in a different mix
A fee charged by the stock exchange on each unit she holds
Mostly the fund's expense ratio, plus small tracking effects
why: An index fund has no stock picking to get wrong. Its shares come from the index list.
If it held different shares it would not be an index fund. It copies the index in the same weights.
The fund's costs are in the expense ratio. Nothing like a per-unit exchange fee is charged to her.
An index fund's return is the index return minus its costs and a little tracking error.

q: Rohan says: "If index funds are cheap and active funds lag, why hold any active fund?" Which reply is sound?
opts: Index for the core, active where managers have more room
Hold only active funds, as managers add value in every segment
Hold only index funds, since they never fall as active funds do
Index funds suit only beginners; active funds suit experts
why: Passive suits efficient areas like large caps, while active has more room in less crowded segments such as small caps.
In efficient areas such as large caps many active funds have struggled to beat their index after costs.
An index fund falls whenever its index falls. Cost is lower, but the risk of the market remains.
Skill level does not decide this. The choice is about which segment and what it costs.

q: Meena has ₹10 lakh in a Nifty index fund and the Nifty falls 30%. Which sentence fits best?
opts: Her fund will fall less, since an index fund holds only top shares
Her fund will stay near ₹10 lakh, since its costs are so low
Her fund will show about ₹7 lakh, since it falls with the index
Her fund will show a loss only if the fund manager makes errors
why: Holding top shares does not protect a fund. If the index drops 30%, those shares drop with it.
Low cost helps over many years, but it does not shield a fund from a falling market.
An index fund tracks the index, so about 30% less, minus tiny costs. Passive does not mean safe.
There is no manager error to blame. The fund is built to follow the index down as well as up.

pts: A passive fund copies an index. Its return is about the index return minus cost.
Low cost, not low risk. An index fund falls when its index falls.
Index core for large caps, active where a manager has room.
